title: Solomon Builds the Temple
summary: In the fourth year of his reign, 480 years after the exodus, Solomon begins building the house of the LORD in Jerusalem. The chapter describes its dimensions, porch, side chambers, and cedar paneling, and the inner sanctuary, the Most Holy Place, a perfect cube overlaid with gold, where two great olive-wood cherubim stand with outstretched wings. In the middle of the building account, the word of the LORD comes to Solomon, promising to dwell among Israel if he obeys, and the work is finished after seven years.
story: This is the moment the Bible has been building toward since the exodus. At Sinai, God gave instructions for a portable tent-sanctuary, the tabernacle, so that he could dwell among his people on the move (Exodus 25:8). Now, with Israel settled and at rest, that tent gives way to a permanent house in the city God chose. The date in verse 1 deliberately ties the temple to the exodus, as if to say the rescue from Egypt reaches its goal here. Yet the chapter doesn't let the building become an idol. In the middle of the construction report, God speaks: the promise of his presence depends not on cedar and gold but on obedience. The temple will stand for nearly four hundred years, until Babylon destroys it in 587 or 586 BC, and the first readers of Kings read this chapter knowing it was gone.
historical:
Solomon's fourth year is usually dated to about 966 BC. The figure of 480 years since the exodus is a key text in debates about when the exodus happened. Read straightforwardly, it places the exodus around 1446 BC, the so-called early date. Many scholars who favor a later exodus, around the thirteenth century BC, read the number as twelve generations of forty years each, a schematic figure, and note that an actual generation was often closer to twenty-five years. Both views are held by careful scholars. The month of Ziv (verse 1) fell in spring, roughly April to May, and Bul (verse 38) in autumn, roughly October to November; these are old Canaanite month names, which the narrator explains with numbered months.

No remains of Solomon's temple have been excavated, since the Temple Mount area is not open to excavation and later building has covered it. But its plan closely resembles temples found elsewhere in the region, especially the Iron Age temple at Ain Dara in northern Syria and a temple at Tell Tayinat in southern Turkey, which also have a porch, a main hall, and an inner shrine in a line. A cubit was about eighteen inches (roughly forty-five centimeters), so the main building was about ninety feet long, thirty feet wide, and forty-five feet high: not enormous by modern standards, but richly finished.
cultural:
An ancient temple was understood as a god's house, not a meeting hall for worshipers. Ordinary Israelites gathered in the courtyards outside, where the altar of sacrifice stood; only priests entered the main hall, and only the high priest entered the Most Holy Place, once a year (Leviticus 16). The building was arranged in zones of increasing holiness, from courtyard to hall to inner sanctuary, following the pattern of the tabernacle.

The decoration carried meaning. Cherubim were winged guardian figures associated with God's throne and presence; the ark itself was topped with two small cherubim (Exodus 25:18-22). Palm trees, gourds, and open flowers, carved throughout and overlaid with gold, turned the interior into a stylized garden. Many interpreters see an echo of Eden, where cherubim guarded the way to the tree of life (Genesis 3:24): the temple was a place where the presence of God, lost in the garden, could be approached again. The ban on hearing iron tools at the building site (verse 7) recalls the law that altars were not to be built of stones shaped with tools (Exodus 20:25), keeping the holy place quiet and set apart.
literary: The chapter reads like an architect's and builder's record: measurements, materials, and methods, with precise dimensions for each part. Its structure moves from outside to inside, from the main building and side chambers (verses 2-10) to the paneling and inner sanctuary (verses 15-22), then to the cherubim and the carvings and doors (verses 23-35). The phrase Solomon built the temple and finished it appears in verses 9 and 14, and verse 38 closes with the temple finished in every detail. God's word in verses 11-13 is set right in the middle of the construction account, interrupting it, so that the reader cannot miss the point: the building matters only if God dwells there, and his dwelling is tied to covenant faithfulness. The perfect cube of the Most Holy Place (twenty by twenty by twenty cubits) expresses completeness and holiness through form.

outline.t: The date: 480 years after the exodus
The main building, porch, windows, and side chambers
The word of the LORD: obedience and presence
Cedar paneling, the inner sanctuary, and gold
Carvings, doors, and the inner courtyard

doctrines.note: The temple's zones of increasing holiness, the gold-covered inner sanctuary, and the guarding cherubim teach that God is holy and cannot be approached casually. His presence is a gift and also a danger to the careless.
God's promise to dwell among Israel and not forsake them is tied to Solomon's obedience. The temple does not guarantee God's presence; covenant faithfulness does.
God wants to dwell among his people. The Bible's story moves from Eden to the tabernacle to the temple and finally to the new creation, all expressing God's desire to live with those he made.

words.note: Shakan, to dwell or settle. God promises, I will dwell among the Israelites (verse 13). From this verb comes mishkan, the tabernacle, and later Jewish tradition used shekinah for God's dwelling presence. It speaks of God making his home among his people.

Devir, inner sanctuary, the innermost room of the temple, also called the Most Holy Place. It housed the ark and the cherubim. The word may be related to the back or rear of the building. It was the heart of Israel's worship, entered only once a year by the high priest.

Keruv, cherub (plural cherubim). These winged guardian creatures appear at Eden's gate, on the ark's cover, and in Ezekiel's visions. In the temple two huge cherubim spread their wings over the place of the ark, picturing God's heavenly throne. They are not the chubby infants of later art.

Azav, to leave or forsake. God promises not to abandon his people Israel (verse 13). The same verb is used when Israel forsakes the LORD, and the book of Kings will show God's patience tested by repeated abandonment on Israel's side.

christ: The temple was the place where heaven and earth met, where God's presence dwelt among his people and sacrifice made approach possible. The New Testament presents Jesus as the fulfillment of what the temple pointed to. John says the Word became flesh and dwelt among us (John 1:14), and Jesus speaks of his own body as the temple (John 2:19-21). When Jesus died, the curtain of the temple was torn in two from top to bottom (Matthew 27:51), which the letter to the Hebrews understands as opening the way into the holy place through his flesh (Hebrews 10:19-20). The Most Holy Place, a perfect cube covered in gold, finds a striking echo in Revelation's picture of the new Jerusalem, a city laid out as a cube and made of pure gold, where there is no temple because God and the Lamb are its temple (Revelation 21:16-22). These are the New Testament's own connections.

hard.q: Does the 480 years of verse 1 settle the date of the exodus?
hard.a: It is one of the main pieces of evidence, but it is interpreted in more than one way. Those who hold the early date (around 1446 BC) take the number as a literal count of years and point to other texts that seem to support it, such as Judges 11:26. Those who hold a later date (in the thirteenth century BC) point to archaeological and historical considerations, including the city named Rameses in Exodus 1:11, and suggest that 480 is a round figure built from twelve generations of forty years, forty being a common biblical number for a generation. Both positions are held by scholars who take the Bible's history seriously. What the verse clearly does is link the temple to the exodus, presenting it as the fulfillment of God's rescue of Israel from Egypt.

questions: God interrupted the building project to say that his presence depends on obedience, not architecture. Where might you be trusting the structures of religion more than God himself?
The temple was designed to show both God's nearness and his holiness. Which of those do you find easier to believe, and why?
The temple interior looked like a golden garden. What does it suggest to you that the place of God's presence was made to recall Eden?
